title: The Invention of the Telephone
description: An encyclopedia-style article on how the telephone was invented and how it changed communication.

image.caption: An early telephone: the speaker talked into the mouthpiece and listened at the earpiece.

paragraphs: Before the telephone, the fastest way to send a message over a long distance was the electric telegraph. It sent short signals along a wire, which a trained operator had to translate into words. It could not carry a human voice.

In 1876, Alexander Graham Bell received a patent for a machine that could send speech along a wire. Bell had spent years teaching deaf students, and his interest in sound and hearing helped him understand how a voice could be turned into an electrical signal.

sections.heading: The first call
paragraphs: On 10 March 1876, Bell spoke into his new instrument to his assistant, Thomas Watson, who was in another room. His words were: "Mr Watson, come here, I want to see you." Watson heard the message clearly, and the first telephone call had been made.
Other inventors were working on similar ideas at the same time, and there were long legal arguments about who deserved the credit. However, Bell's patent was accepted by the courts.

sections.heading: A changing world
paragraphs: Within a few years, telephone lines connected homes and businesses in many cities. Operators at exchanges connected each call by hand. Today, mobile phones carry voices, text and pictures around the world in less than a second, but they still depend on the same basic idea: changing sound into a signal and back again.
